teaser: A tiny pen ball opens a big question: hard, tough, or both?
title: Tungsten Carbide
question: Can something be very hard, but still break?
idea: Hard means resisting scratches and dents. Tough means resisting cracks and breaks. A small hard carbide tip and a tougher steel body can work together.

curiosity.intro: A little piece can have a very particular job. What job needs hard? What job needs tough?
curiosity.carryForward: Follow a pen ball, a soap scratch and a snowy path. Keep two useful words.

questions.question: What is hiding at the end of a pen?
questions.notice: Look for the tiny round ball where ink meets paper.
questions.say: The tiny ball in many ballpoint pens is tungsten carbide. It rolls ink onto paper and resists wear. People make this material by joining tungsten with carbon, then pressing powder and heating it very hot. This heating step is called sintering. Usually, a little cobalt metal binds the grains together: cemented carbide.
questions.try: Trace the rolling ball in the picture, then point to the line it leaves.

questions.question: What can a scratch tell us?
questions.notice: Big moves the craft stick across soap on a tray. Little watches and records.
questions.say: A harder thing can scratch a softer thing. Hard means resisting scratches and dents. Tungsten carbide is one of the hardest materials people make. It is also heavy for its size. The soap test lets Little see a surface give way.
questions.try: Predict what mark Big’s craft stick will leave in the soap. Record what you notice.

questions.question: Does hard always mean tough?
questions.notice: Compare the chalk pieces with the eraser bending in Big’s hands.
questions.say: Tough means resisting cracks or breaks when bumped, bent or dropped. Hard and tough are different. Chalk snaps when bent; an eraser can bend back. Tungsten carbide is very hard but less tough than steel. It is brittle enough to chip if knocked hard.
questions.try: Say which test gives a clue about a surface, and which gives a clue about breaking.

questions.question: Why give a hard tip a tough body?
questions.notice: Little’s sketch joins a small tip to a larger body.
questions.say: Engineers often join a carbide tip to a tougher steel body, as on saw teeth and some masonry drill bits. The tip resists wear while the steel takes bumps. Carbide also appears in some ski-pole and hiking-pole tips and ice-grip studs. Choose a material for its job: hard, tough, or both.
questions.try: Choose a job for the tip, then a job for the body.

outline.arc: A resting carbide tip starts a question; a pen reveals its everyday use; a soap scratch and chalk/eraser comparison separate hard from tough; pole tips and a steel-backed tooth show how engineers choose materials.

beatIntents.intent: Introduce a resting carbide-tipped tooth on linen and the question of hard versus tough; no tool is operated or held.
Discover the rolling carbide ball in an ordinary pen; prose explains joining tungsten with carbon, pressing powder and heating, with a cobalt binder.
Big performs a gentle craft-stick scratch on soap over a tray; Little only predicts, watches and records.
Compare two already separated chalk pieces with Big gently bending an eraser; no flying pieces, powder cloud or child handling.
Follow the pair onto a calm snowy path, with pole tips planted into the ground; small carbide tips serve a specific job.
Return to the shared notebook and compare a hard carbide tip with the tougher steel body supporting it; leave a material-choice question open.

beats.title: A small tip, a big question
beats.passage: A gray tip rested on a cloth. “Could that little piece do a big job?” asked Little Wonderer. “It is tungsten carbide,” said Big. “A material is what something is made of. This one is heavy for its size and very hard. But being hard does not mean it can never break.”
beats.prompt: What might hard tell us about this little tip?

beats.title: The ball inside a pen
beats.passage: Little found another clue in a pen. Many ballpoint pens have a tiny tungsten-carbide ball that rolls ink onto paper. People make carbide by joining tungsten, a metal, with carbon. They press the powder and heat it very hot. A little cobalt metal usually holds the grains together, like glue.
beats.prompt: Why could a pen ball need to resist wear?

beats.title: A line in the soap
beats.passage: Big set soap and a wooden craft stick on a tray. Little guessed what would happen, then watched. Big gently drew the stick across the soap. A scratch appeared: a small line dug into the surface. Hard means resisting scratches and dents. The soap gave way to the harder stick.
beats.prompt: What did the scratch show about the soap?

beats.title: A bend and a break
beats.passage: Would a hard surface also resist breaking? Big gently bent chalk over the tray. It snapped. A rubber eraser bent and came back. Tough means resisting cracks and breaks from bumps or bends. Brittle things can chip or crack. Tungsten carbide is very hard, but a strong knock can chip it.
beats.prompt: How are resisting scratches and resisting breaks different?

beats.title: A little grip in the snow
beats.passage: On a snowy walk, Little noticed the tips of their hiking poles. The tip is the small end that meets the ground. Some pole tips and ice-grip studs use carbide to bite into ice. “The hard part is only a tiny piece!” Little said. “Just where it is useful,” said Big.
beats.prompt: Why put carbide just at a pole’s tip?

beats.title: Hard, tough, or both
beats.passage: Back at the notebook, Big showed a saw-tooth picture. A small carbide tip joined a steel body. The hard tip resists wear; the tougher steel takes bumps without cracking as easily. “Two materials, two jobs,” Little said. “Do I need it hard, tough, or both?”
beats.prompt: Why might one object need two materials?

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Hard is resistance to scratches and dents. Tough is resistance to cracking and breaking. One does not guarantee the other.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Chalk snapped, while the rubber eraser bent back. This compares how they respond to bending, not their scratch hardness.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: A hard carbide tip resists wear. A tougher steel body supports it and takes bumps.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept one sensible command, spoken, dictated or written. Example: Ask Big to hold the soap and gently drag the craft stick across it.

parentGuidance: Age 8 / Grade 3 reading and Grade 2 math. A grown-up leads every step of the optional household test; the child watches, predicts and records. Work over a tray and keep faces back. Use only soap, a smooth wooden craft stick, chalk and a flexible rubber eraser. The grown-up holds the soap and gently drags the craft stick across it, then separately bends chalk gently over the tray and bends the eraser. Stop if extra force is needed; keep crumbs on the tray. No knives, nails, glass, ceramic tiles, files, drills, saws or sharp tools; use nothing that makes shards. Never touch real saw blades or drill bits. Do not scratch with a pen tip or any tungsten carbide. WC is tungsten joined with carbon; carbide is manufactured, rather than mined as a finished tool material. Pressing and sintering usually use a cobalt binder, not household glue. Hardness and toughness vary with grain size, binder and grade. The bench gives qualitative comparisons, not measured tests or a promise that every bump chips carbide. Its scratch contact is a carbide point; on carbide it leaves no visible mark under the shown light contact. Its bump is strong enough to reveal different responses. The chalk/eraser activity is a separate bending comparison, not a ranking of toughness by measurement. Materials differ in softness as well as brittleness. Tools stay resting in pictures. Welcome dictation and a pause at any time.
